items.question: In the normal (non-degraded) AFCS configuration for IFR or VFR operations (PSAS1 and PSAS2, AP1 and AP2, ATT Mode), what is the maximum VNE?
options: 165 KIAS
120 KIAS
150 KIAS
106 KIAS
items.explanation: With the full normal AFCS configuration engaged (PSAS1/2, AP1/2, ATT Mode, cyclic and rudder trim), maximum VNE is 165 KIAS — and it stays 165 KIAS with just one AP, or in SAS Mode, as long as both PSAS1 and PSAS2 are still operating. VNE drops to 120 KIAS only when a single PSAS channel is paired with both APs in ATT Mode, or when a single PSAS/AP pair operates in SAS Mode.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: REQUIRED EQUIPMENT (p.1-1/1-2)

items.question: What is the minimum flight crew specified in the S-92 RFM?
options: Two pilots
One pilot
One pilot and one flight engineer
Two pilots and a flight engineer
items.explanation: The RFM specifies a minimum flight crew of two pilots; the Pilot in Command may occupy either cockpit seat.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: MINIMUM FLIGHT CREW (p.1-2)

items.question: What limitation applies to the Enhanced Ground Proximity Warning System (EGPWS)?
options: Navigation must not be predicated upon the use of EGPWS information
EGPWS Low Altitude Mode is mandatory whenever operating in IMC
The Terrain and Obstacle display may be used for routine navigation
EGPWS must be turned off during all offshore approaches
items.explanation: The EGPWS does not include power lines in its database, so navigation must never be predicated upon EGPWS information; the terrain/obstacle display is an awareness tool only, not a routine navigation reference.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: ENHANCED GROUND PROXIMITY WARNING SYSTEM (EGPWS) (p.1-2)

items.question: For RNP5/BRNAV operation with the FMS, usable navigation information must be received from which source(s)?
options: GPS, or one VOR/DME, or multiple DMEs
GPS only, with no other navaid substitution permitted
Two VOR stations simultaneously
ADF and DME only
items.explanation: RNP5/BRNAV is approved provided the FMS receives usable navigation information from GPS, or from one VOR/DME, or from multiple DMEs.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: FMS OPERATIONAL APPROVALS (p.1-3)

items.question: Which of the following is explicitly prohibited under FLIGHT LIMITS in the S-92 RFM?
options: Practice touchdown autorotations
Simulated single-engine approaches
Practice run-on landings
Simulated hydraulic-off approaches
items.explanation: FLIGHT LIMITS explicitly prohibits practice touchdown autorotations, along with aerobatic maneuvers and 360° hovering turns in less than 12 seconds.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: FLIGHT LIMITS (p.1-5)

items.question: What is the maximum crosswind component for Category A ground level helipad takeoffs and landings?
options: 22 knots
35 knots
30 knots
15 knots
items.explanation: Category A ground level helipad takeoffs and landings are limited to 22 knots of crosswind component; Category A horizontal takeoffs and landings allow up to 35 knots.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: FLIGHT LIMITS (p.1-5)

items.question: What is the maximum bank angle permitted with one primary flight control servo inoperative?
items.explanation: With one primary flight control servo inoperative, maximum bank angle is limited to 30°.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: FLIGHT LIMITS (p.1-5)

items.question: With low fuel light(s) illuminated, which steady-state pitch attitudes must be avoided?
options: More than 10° nose up or more than 5° nose down
More than 5° nose up or more than 10° nose down
More than 15° nose up or nose down
Any pitch attitude change is prohibited
items.explanation: With low fuel light(s) illuminated, the RFM directs avoiding steady state pitch attitudes in excess of 10° nose up and lower than 5° nose down.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: FLIGHT LIMITS (p.1-5)

items.question: What are the slope landing limits stated in the S-92 RFM?
options: 10° nose up or down slope, 13° left or right side up-slope
13° nose up or down slope, 10° left or right side up-slope
5° in any direction
15° nose up or down slope, 15° lateral
items.explanation: Slope landing limits are 10° nose up or down slope, and 13° left or right side of the aircraft up-slope.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: FLIGHT LIMITS (p.1-5)

items.question: If VNE power on is less than 120 KIAS, what VNE power off value applies?
options: The lower VNE power-on value applies for the power-off case as well
VNE power off remains fixed at 120 KIAS regardless of VNE power on
VNE power off is always 165 KIAS
VNE power off is undefined below 120 KIAS
items.explanation: VNE power off is normally 120 KIAS, but if VNE power on is less than 120 KIAS, that lower value applies for the power-off case as well.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: AIRSPEED LIMITS (p.1-7)

items.question: What is the maximum airspeed with one engine inoperative?
options: 120 KIAS
165 KIAS
150 KIAS
90 KIAS
items.explanation: Maximum airspeed with one engine inoperative is 120 KIAS, the same limit that applies with SAS, AP, or primary flight control servo degradations.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: AIRSPEED LIMITS (p.1-7)

items.question: What is the maximum airspeed with the hydraulic boost system inoperative?
options: 120 KIAS
165 KIAS
90 KIAS
80 KIAS
items.explanation: Maximum airspeed with the hydraulic boost inoperative is 120 KIAS.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: AIRSPEED LIMITS (p.1-7)

items.question: What is the maximum groundspeed for taxi operations and for brake application?
options: 35 knots
50 knots
65 knots
20 knots
items.explanation: Maximum groundspeed for taxi operations is 35 knots, and maximum groundspeed for brake application is also 35 knots.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: AIRSPEED LIMITS (p.1-7/1-8)

items.question: What is the maximum enroute altitude limit stated under ALTITUDE LIMITS?
options: 15,000 feet density altitude
20,000 feet pressure altitude
10,000 feet pressure altitude
12,000 feet density altitude
items.explanation: Enroute altitude is limited to 15,000 feet density altitude. Flight in icing conditions with RIPS installed is limited to 10,000 feet pressure altitude, a separate limit.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: ALTITUDE LIMITS (p.1-8)

items.question: What is the ambient temperature operating range for the S-92 per AMBIENT TEMPERATURE LIMITS?
options: -40°C to ISA +35°C
-25°C to ISA +30°C
-50°C to ISA +40°C
0°C to ISA +35°C
items.explanation: The ambient temperature operating range is -40°C to ISA +35°C. Operation is also prohibited if the shut-down rotorcraft is exposed below -25°C for longer than 1 hour without warming or use of the cold weather pre-heat kit.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: AMBIENT TEMPERATURE LIMITS (p.1-8)

items.question: What is the maximum takeoff and landing weight of the S-92 per Part 1 WEIGHT LIMITS?
options: 26,500 pounds
24,500 pounds
28,000 pounds
22,000 pounds
items.explanation: Maximum takeoff and landing weight is 26,500 pounds (12,020 kilograms); minimum operating weight is 16,200 pounds.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: WEIGHT LIMITS (p.1-9)

items.question: What is the maximum continuous torque (Q%) rating for dual-engine operation?
items.explanation: Dual-engine maximum continuous torque is 100% Q. 120% Q is the single-engine (OEI) maximum continuous rating, and 141% Q is the OEI 30-second rating — not the dual-engine continuous value.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: PROPULSION AND DRIVE SYSTEM LIMITS (p.1-18)

items.question: What is the single-engine (OEI) 30-second torque limit?
items.explanation: The OEI 30-second torque limit is 141% Q. 120% Q is OEI maximum continuous, and 156% Q is the OEI 5-second transient limit.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: PROPULSION AND DRIVE SYSTEM LIMITS (p.1-18)

items.question: Which Np/Nr ranges must be avoided for prolonged operation per the RFM?
options: 40% to 55% only
items.explanation: Prolonged operation must be avoided in the 36% to 49% Np/Nr range (tail rotor drive shaft critical range) and the 56% to 67% range (engine power turbine critical range).
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: Np/Nr AVOID RANGES (p.1-18)

items.question: Under FUEL CROSSFEED LIMITS, when is fuel crossfeed permitted for Category A operations?
options: Emergency operation only
Cruise flight only
Anytime in flight
Ground operations only
items.explanation: Fuel crossfeed for Category A operations is limited to emergency operation only. Category B fuel crossfeed is limited to cruise flight only — a distinct, category-specific limit.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: FUEL CROSSFEED LIMITS (p.1-19)

items.question: Per FUEL TEMPERATURE LIMITS, what is the maximum permitted fuel temperature for Jet A (JP-5, No. 3 Jet Fuel) or Jet A-1 (JP-8)?
items.explanation: Jet A and Jet A-1 have a maximum fuel temperature of 57°C (135°F). Jet B (JP-4) is lower, at 16°C (60°F); all three fuels share the same minimum of -40°C (-40°F).
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: FUEL TEMPERATURE LIMITS (p.1-20)

items.question: At what fuel temperature does FUEL TEMPERATURE LIMITS require a fuel anti-icing additive?
options: Below -20°C (-4°F)
Below 0°C (32°F)
Below -40°C (-40°F)
Above 57°C (135°F)
items.explanation: Fuel anti-icing additives are required at fuel temperatures below -20°C (-4°F); above that threshold, heating or anti-icing additive is not required.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: FUEL TEMPERATURE LIMITS (p.1-20)

items.question: What is the total fuel quantity for a gravity refuel, per FUEL CAPACITY?
options: 713 US gallons (2700 L)
764 US gallons (2890 L) — that's the pressure refuel figure
4.8 US gallons (18 L) — that's the unusable fuel amount
4,830 lb (2190 kg) — that's the Jet A weight at pressure refuel
items.explanation: Gravity refuel total capacity is 713 US gallons (2700 liters); pressure refuel is higher, at 764 US gallons (2890 liters). Of the total quantity, 4.8 gallons (18 liters) is unusable.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: FUEL CAPACITY (p.1-20)

items.question: Why does the RFM recommend servicing engines only with approved Type II oils rather than Type I?
options: Type II oils withstand higher operating temperatures and have improved anti-coking characteristics
Type II oils are lower viscosity, which reduces oil pressure
Type I oils are prohibited from ever being mixed with Type II
Type II oils are required only at ambient temperatures below -40°C
items.explanation: Type II oils can withstand higher operating temperatures and have improved anti-coking characteristics. They also have higher viscosity than Type I, which may result in slightly higher oil pressure under similar speed/temperature conditions — the opposite of "lower viscosity, reduces pressure."
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: APPROVED OILS (p.1-21)

items.question: According to APPROVED OILS, is mixing Type I and Type II engine oils authorized?
options: Yes, though it is recommended to use only one type when possible
No, mixing oil types is not authorized under any circumstance
Only Type II may be topped up with Type I, never the reverse
Mixing is authorized in the engine only, never in the transmission
items.explanation: The RFM authorizes mixing of brand names as well as mixing of Type I and Type II oils, while recommending that only one type be used when possible.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: APPROVED OILS (p.1-21)

items.question: Per BACK-TO-BACK STARTING LIMIT, above +15°C (+59°F), what starting cycle is permitted before a 30-minute cooling period is required?
options: 2 consecutive starts, 5-minute cooling, then 2 more consecutive starts
4 consecutive starts, 15-minute cooling, then 4 more consecutive starts — that's the +15°C-or-less rule
3 consecutive starts, 10-minute cooling, then 3 more
Unlimited starts as long as 5 minutes separates each one
items.explanation: Above +15°C (+59°F): 2 consecutive starts, 5-minute cooling, 2 more consecutive starts, then a 30-minute cooling period before repeating. At +15°C or below, the limit is more permissive: 4 starts, 15-minute cooling, 4 more starts, then 30 minutes.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: STARTER LIMITS, BACK-TO-BACK STARTING LIMIT (p.1-22)

items.question: At or below +15°C (+59°F), how many consecutive engine starts are permitted before a 15-minute cooling period, per BACK-TO-BACK STARTING LIMIT?
options: 2 — that's the above-+15°C rule
items.explanation: At +15°C (+59°F) or less, the cycle is 4 consecutive starts, 15-minute cooling, 4 more consecutive starts, then 30-minute cooling, then repeat.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: STARTER LIMITS, BACK-TO-BACK STARTING LIMIT (p.1-22)

items.question: What is the STARTER MOTORING LIMIT cycle?
options: 2 minutes on, 5 minutes off, 2 minutes on, 30 minutes off, then repeat
5 minutes on, 2 minutes off, repeat indefinitely
4 minutes on, 15 minutes off, repeat
30 seconds on, 5 minutes off, repeat
items.explanation: Starter motoring limit is 2 minutes on / 5 minutes off, then 2 minutes on / 30 minutes off, then the cycle repeats.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: STARTER MOTORING LIMIT (p.1-22)

items.question: Per ENGINE AND APU INFLIGHT STARTING, APU starts and continuous operation in flight are restricted to airspeeds below what value?
options: 150 KIAS
165 KIAS — that's VNE
120 KIAS — that's the OEI/power-off VNE
100 KIAS — that's the dual-engine torque break airspeed
items.explanation: Engine starts in flight are authorized throughout the complete aircraft operating envelope, but APU starts and continuous APU operation are restricted to airspeeds less than 150 KIAS.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: ENGINE AND APU INFLIGHT STARTING (p.1-22)

items.question: What is the maximum MGB oil temperature, per MGB OIL TEMPERATURE LIMITS?
options: 120°C — that's the top of the continuous range
149°C — that's the engine oil maximum, a different system
132°C — that's the engine oil continuous maximum, a different system
items.explanation: MGB oil temperature: continuous 0° to 120°C, precautionary 120° to 130°C, maximum 130°C. Don't confuse it with the separate engine oil temperature limits (continuous to 132°C, maximum 149°C).
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: MGB OIL TEMPERATURE LIMITS (p.1-23)

items.question: With Nr at or above 80%, or the aircraft airborne, what is the minimum MGB oil pressure per MGB OIL PRESSURE LIMITS?
options: 35 psi
45 psi — that's the bottom of the continuous range
10 psi — that's the minimum for low-Nr ground conditions
70 psi — that's the top of the continuous range
items.explanation: With Nr ≥ 80% or the aircraft in the air: minimum 35 psi, precautionary 35–45 psi, continuous 45–70 psi, precautionary 70–130 psi, maximum 130 psi. The minimum is lower (10 psi) only in the two ground-operation, lower-Nr conditions.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: MGB OIL PRESSURE LIMITS (p.1-23)

items.question: What is the normal operating rotor speed range (power on) for dual-engine operation, per ROTOR SPEED LIMITS?
options: 100% to 106% — that's the OEI normal range
95% to 104% — that's the dual-engine precautionary range
106% to 110% — that's the overall precautionary range
items.explanation: Power-on normal operating rotor speed is 104% to 106% for dual engine, and 100% to 106% for OEI — two distinct ranges depending on engine state.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: ROTOR SPEED LIMITS, POWER ON (p.1-24)

items.question: What are the power-on OEI rotor speed transient limits?
options: 90% transient minimum; 80% transient at touchdown during an OEI landing
95% transient minimum; 100% at touchdown
80% transient minimum; 90% at touchdown
85% transient minimum; 95% at touchdown
items.explanation: Power-on: transient minimum OEI is 90%, and transient at touchdown during an OEI landing is 80% — a lower, specifically-carved-out allowance for that one phase of flight.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: ROTOR SPEED LIMITS, POWER ON (p.1-24)

items.question: At what power-off rotor speed does the minimum threshold ("LOW ROTOR" aural alert) occur?
options: 80% — that's the power-off transient minimum
110% — that's the power-off maximum
90% — that's the power-on OEI transient minimum
items.explanation: Power off: maximum 110%, minimum ("LOW ROTOR" aural alert) 95%, transient minimum 80%.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: ROTOR SPEED LIMITS, POWER OFF (p.1-24)

items.question: What must be done before applying the rotor brake, per the ROTOR TURNING CAUTION?
options: Both engines must be shut down
At least one engine must remain at idle
Both engines must be at flight idle, not shut down
The APU must be running to supply hydraulic power
items.explanation: CAUTION: both engines must be shut down before applying the rotor brake.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: ROTOR BRAKE LIMITS, ROTOR TURNING (p.1-25)

items.question: What is the maximum rotor speed for an EMERGENCY rotor brake application, with both engines shut down?
options: 40% Nr — that's the recommended speed for a normal rotor brake application
95% Nr
110% Nr — that's the overall maximum rotor speed
items.explanation: Recommended rotor speed for a normal rotor brake application is 40% Nr or below; the maximum rotor speed for an emergency rotor brake application, with both engines shut down, is 105% Nr.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: ROTOR BRAKE LIMITS, ROTOR TURNING (p.1-25)

items.question: What is the normal operating pressure range for the S-92 hydraulic system, per HYDRAULIC SYSTEM LIMITS?
options: 2000 ± 1000 psi — that's the System 3 depress condition only
3500 psi minimum, with no stated upper bound
items.explanation: Hydraulic system limits: depress (System 3 only) 2000 ± 1000 psi, minimum 3500 psi, normal 3500 to 4200 psi, maximum 4200 psi.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: HYDRAULIC SYSTEM LIMITS (p.1-25)

items.question: Per APPROVED HYDRAULIC FLUID, what restriction applies to MIL-PRF-83282 fluid?
options: It may only be used at ambient temperatures above -32°C (-25°F)
It may only be used at ambient temperatures below -32°C (-25°F)
It is prohibited from being mixed with MIL-PRF-87257
It may only be used in System 3
items.explanation: MIL-PRF-87257 is authorized at all approved ambient temperatures; MIL-PRF-83282 may only be used at ambient temperatures above -32°C (-25°F).
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: APPROVED HYDRAULIC FLUID (p.1-25)

items.question: Per the INSTRUMENT MARKINGS for engine oil pressure, what is the idle minimum pressure band?
options: 20 to 30 psi
30 to 100 psi — that's the continuous band
100 to 120 psi — that's the 5-minute band
120 psi — that's the maximum
items.explanation: Engine oil pressure markings: 120 psi maximum, 100–120 psi 5-minute band, 30–100 psi continuous, and 20–30 psi idle minimum.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: INSTRUMENT MARKINGS, Figure 1-6 Sheet 1 (p.1-26)

items.question: Maximum continuous dual-engine torque may exceed 100% on one engine up to what maximum, provided the sum of both engines' torque does not exceed 200%?
options: 110%, provided the other engine's torque is proportionally less than 100%
120% — that's the single-engine maximum continuous rating
141% — that's the OEI 30-second rating
100% — no engine may exceed the normal continuous value
items.explanation: Maximum continuous dual-engine torque may exceed 100% on one engine to a maximum of 110%, provided the torque on the other engine is proportionally less than 100% and the sum of the individual torque values does not exceed 200%.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: PROPULSION AND DRIVE SYSTEM LIMITS, table note (p.1-18)

items.question: At airspeeds greater than 100 KIAS, dual-engine maximum continuous torque is reduced from 100% to 86% Q. Why?
options: To limit flight control loads at high speed and preserve dynamic component replacement times — it is explicitly not a gearbox limit
Because 86% Q is the gearbox's structural limit above 100 KIAS
Because it matches the single-engine continuous rating
There is no reduction above 100 KIAS — 100% Q still applies
items.explanation: Table note (1): "86% Q is not a gearbox limit. Its purpose is to limit flight control loads at high speed thereby preserving dynamic component replacement times."
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: PROPULSION AND DRIVE SYSTEM LIMITS, note (1) (p.1-18)

items.question: What is the 5-minute takeoff TGT limit for dual-engine operation, and how does it compare to maximum continuous?
options: 995°C for 5 minutes, versus 935°C maximum continuous
935°C for 5 minutes, versus 995°C maximum continuous
1000°C for 5 minutes, versus 988°C maximum continuous
988°C for 5 minutes, versus 935°C maximum continuous
items.explanation: Dual-engine TGT: maximum continuous 935°C, 30-minute (hover only) 988°C, takeoff (5 min) 995°C, transient (12 sec) 1003°C.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: PROPULSION AND DRIVE SYSTEM LIMITS (p.1-18); INSTRUMENT MARKINGS Sheet 5 (p.1-30)

items.question: What is the single-engine (OEI) 30-second TGT limit?
options: 1006°C — that's the OEI 2-minute TGT limit
988°C — that's the single-engine maximum continuous TGT
1000°C — that's the maximum starting TGT
items.explanation: Single-engine TGT: maximum continuous 988°C, OEI 2-minute 1006°C, OEI 30-second 1049°C, maximum starting (peak) 1000°C.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: PROPULSION AND DRIVE SYSTEM LIMITS (p.1-18); INSTRUMENT MARKINGS Sheet 5 (p.1-30)

items.question: At what Np and Ng values do the automatic overspeed trips activate, per the PROPULSION AND DRIVE SYSTEM LIMITS notes?
options: Np at 120%, Ng at 108.5%
Np at 110%, Ng at 103.7%
Np at 106%, Ng at 99.9%
Np at 116%, Ng at 103.7%
items.explanation: "Np overspeed trip is at 120%. Ng overspeed trip is at 108.5%." These are automatic protective trips, distinct from the normal rated Np/Ng operating values in the same table.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: PROPULSION AND DRIVE SYSTEM LIMITS, table notes (p.1-18)

items.question: What is the maximum allowable cabin floor loading, and how does a heavy-duty floor change it?
options: 75 lb/sq ft (366 kg/m²) standard, 200 lb/sq ft (976 kg/m²) with a heavy-duty floor
200 lb/sq ft standard, 75 lb/sq ft with a heavy-duty floor
1,000 lb (454 kg) combined, regardless of floor type
300 lb (136 kg) standard, 1,000 lb with a heavy-duty floor
items.explanation: Maximum allowable cabin floor loading is 75 lb/sq ft (366 kg/m²); with a heavy-duty floor installed, it rises to 200 lb/sq ft (976 kg/m²).
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: CABIN FLOOR LOADING LIMITS (p.1-17)

items.question: With the rear ramp area configured for stowing baggage, what is the maximum combined load, and the maximum shelf load?
options: 1,000 lb (454 kg) combined; 300 lb (136 kg) maximum shelf load
300 lb (136 kg) combined; 1,000 lb maximum shelf load
75 lb/sq ft combined; no shelf load limit is stated
2,000 lb (907 kg) combined; 500 lb maximum shelf load
items.explanation: With the aft cabin cargo bulkhead and shelf installed, the maximum combined load is 1,000 lb (454 kg); the maximum shelf load is 300 lb (136 kg); the maximum floor ramp load is also 1,000 lb (454 kg), at up to 200 lb/sq ft (976.5 kg/m²).
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: BAGGAGE LOADING LIMIT (p.1-17)

items.question: Per the CAUTION preceding CABIN FLOOR LOADING LIMITS, a fuel-tank imbalance in excess of what value — combined with grossly unbalanced cargo/passenger loading — may put the aircraft outside allowable lateral CG limits?
items.explanation: CAUTION: imbalances in excess of 700 lb (317 kg) between fuel tanks, when combined with grossly unbalanced cargo/passenger loading, may put the aircraft outside of allowable lateral CG limits.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: CABIN FLOOR LOADING LIMITS, preceding CAUTION (p.1-17)

items.question: Per the PROPULSION AND DRIVE SYSTEM LIMITS notes, what happens if the aircraft is flown above 8,000 feet at outside air temperatures below -20°C and the corrected Ng speed limit is reached?
options: The engine will not produce more power; further collective increase will only cause Nr to droop
The FADEC automatically raises the Ng limit to compensate for altitude
An Ng overspeed trip activates immediately
The APU must be started to provide supplemental shaft power
items.explanation: "When flying at altitudes greater than 8,000 feet at outside air temperatures lower than -20 degrees C, it is possible to reach the corrected Ng speed limit of the engines. When this occurs, the engine will not produce more power. The only indication that the pilot will see when reaching this limit is that any further increase in collective will commensurately droop Nr."
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: PROPULSION AND DRIVE SYSTEM LIMITS, table notes (p.1-18)

items.question: What passenger seat limits apply to Category A and Category B operations?
options: Category A: a maximum of 9 passenger seats. Category B: 19 or less
Category A: a maximum of 19 passenger seats. Category B: 9 or less
Category A: a maximum of 19 passenger seats. Category B: no limit
Category A: a maximum of 22 passenger seats. Category B: 12 or less
items.explanation: Types of operation: Category 'A' with a maximum of 19 passenger seats or Category 'B' with 9 or less passenger seats; Day, Night, VFR and IFR.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: TYPES OF OPERATION (p.1-1)

items.question: With the Rotor Ice Protection System (RIPS) installed, up to what altitude is flight in icing conditions approved?
options: 15,000 feet density altitude
10,000 feet pressure altitude
10,000 feet density altitude
5,000 feet pressure altitude
items.explanation: With the Rotor Ice Protection System (RIPS) installed, flight in icing conditions is approved up to 10,000 feet pressure altitude.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: TYPES OF OPERATION (p.1-1)

items.question: Day or night VFR with degraded AFCS: which configuration still allows a maximum VNE of 165 KIAS?
options: PSAS1 or PSAS2, AP1 and AP2, ATT mode, cyclic and rudder trim
PSAS1/AP1 or PSAS2/AP2, SAS mode, functional cyclic trim release
PSAS1 or PSAS2, AP1 or AP2, ATT mode, cyclic trim only
PSAS1 and PSAS2, AP1 and/or AP2, SAS mode, cyclic and rudder trim
items.explanation: Day or night VFR with certain PSAS and/or AP components inoperative: PSAS1 and PSAS2, AP1 or AP2, ATT mode — VNE 165 KIAS; PSAS1 and PSAS2, AP1 and/or AP2, SAS mode — VNE 165 KIAS; PSAS1 or PSAS2, AP1 and AP2, ATT mode — VNE 120 KIAS; PSAS1/AP1 or PSAS2/AP2, SAS mode with functional cyclic trim release — VNE 120 KIAS. Losing a PSAS channel is what drops VNE to 120 KIAS.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: REQUIRED EQUIPMENT (p.1-1)

items.question: What does the RFM say about taking off with a secondary SAS engaged?
options: It is not authorized; secondary SAS may be engaged after an inflight failure of a primary SAS computer
It is authorized in VFR only, with VNE limited to 120 KIAS
It is authorized if both autopilots are engaged in ATT mode
It is authorized after a successful AFCS preflight built in test
items.explanation: NOTE: takeoff with a secondary SAS engaged is not authorized. Secondary SAS may be engaged after an inflight failure of a primary SAS computer. CAUTION: when operating in a degraded AFCS mode, a pilot will be attentive to the flight controls when in ATT mode and will manually control the aircraft when flying in SAS mode.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: REQUIRED EQUIPMENT (p.1-2)

items.question: In a degraded AFCS mode, what does the RFM CAUTION require of the pilot?
options: Fly the aircraft manually in ATT mode, and be attentive to the controls in SAS mode
Keep the autopilot coupled in both modes and monitor the flight director
Be attentive to the flight controls in ATT mode, and fly the aircraft manually in SAS mode
Limit bank to 30° in ATT mode and fly below 80 KIAS in SAS mode
items.explanation: CAUTION: when operating in a degraded AFCS mode, a pilot will be attentive to the flight controls when in ATT mode and will manually control the aircraft when flying in SAS mode.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: REQUIRED EQUIPMENT (p.1-2)

items.question: Which items on the required equipment list are required only for IMC?
options: The APU, the four MFDs and the AFCS
Two DCUs, two primary AC generators and all standby instruments
Two DCUs, the APU and the four MFDs
Two primary AC generators, the AFCS and the APU
items.explanation: Required equipment: 1. Auxiliary power unit. 2. Two Data Concentrator Units (DCUs) (IMC). 3. Four instrument panel MFDs. 4. AFCS. 5. Two primary AC generators (IMC). 6. All standby instruments (IMC). 7. The applicable operators manual on board for all equipment not covered in Part II.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: REQUIRED EQUIPMENT (p.1-1, p.1-2)

items.question: In the S-92 RFM procedures, which seat does the "pilot" occupy, and where may the pilot in command sit?
options: The pilot is in the left seat; the PIC may occupy either seat
The pilot is in the right seat; the PIC may occupy either seat
The pilot is in the right seat; the PIC must occupy the right seat
The pilot is in the left seat; the PIC must occupy the left seat
items.explanation: Minimum flight crew: two pilots. For the procedures in this manual the "pilot" occupies the right cockpit seat and the "copilot" occupies the left cockpit seat. The Pilot in Command (PIC) may occupy either cockpit seat.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: MINIMUM FLIGHT CREW (p.1-2)

items.question: What does the RFM say about EGPWS and power lines?
options: EGPWS warns of power lines only in Low Altitude Mode
EGPWS warns of power lines above 200 feet AGL only
EGPWS gives no power line warnings; power lines are not in its database
EGPWS warns of power lines listed in the FMS database
items.explanation: The EGPWS will not provide power line warnings. Power lines are not included in the EGPWS data base.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: ENHANCED GROUND PROXIMITY WARNING SYSTEM (EGPWS) (p.1-2)

items.question: When may EGPWS Low Altitude Mode be selected in IMC?
options: At any time below 1,000 feet AGL
Only during the final approach segment of an ILS
Only as required for offshore platform IMC approaches or other Special Procedures
Never; it is approved for VMC only, with no exceptions
items.explanation: EGPWS Low Altitude Mode must not be selected when operating under IMC conditions except as required when performing offshore platform IMC Approach Procedures or other Special Procedures.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: ENHANCED GROUND PROXIMITY WARNING SYSTEM (EGPWS) (p.1-2)

items.question: Beyond what latitudes must the pilot manually insert magnetic variation into the FMS?
options: North of 60° N or south of 73° S
North of 70° N or south of 70° S
North of 73° N or south of 60° S
North of 80° N or south of 80° S
items.explanation: When operating north of 73 degrees north latitude or south of 60 degrees south latitude the pilot must manually insert magnetic variation.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: FMS OPERATING LIMITATIONS (p.1-3)

items.question: If the air data input to the FMS is lost, what must the pilot do?
options: Manually insert TAS and altitude every 30 minutes
Manually insert TAS and altitude every 10 minutes
Manually insert groundspeed and heading every 10 minutes
Nothing; the FMS reverts to GPS altitude automatically
items.explanation: When the air data input is lost to the FMS, the pilot must manually insert TAS and Altitude information every 10 minutes.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: FMS OPERATING LIMITATIONS (p.1-3)

items.question: When are IFR en route and terminal navigation with the FMS prohibited?
options: Unless the pilot verifies the database currency or checks each waypoint against current approved data
Unless both the FMS and the EGPWS databases were updated within 7 days
Whenever the FMS is operating in dead reckoning with a valid GPS signal
Unless a second FMS is installed and agrees within 1 nm
items.explanation: IFR En Route and Terminal navigation are prohibited unless the pilot verifies the currency of the data base or verifies each selected waypoint for accuracy by reference to current approved data. Other navigation equipment appropriate to the ground facilities along the route must be installed and operable as required by the operating rules.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: FMS OPERATING LIMITATIONS (p.1-4)

items.question: What limitations apply to FMS dead reckoning and to manually inserted runway coordinates?
options: Dead reckoning is approved for up to 10 minutes; manually inserted runway coordinates are IFR approved
Dead reckoning is approved in VMC; manually inserted runway coordinates need a RAIM check
No navigation predicated on the FMS in dead reckoning; manually inserted runway coordinates are VFR only
No limitation on dead reckoning; manually inserted runway coordinates are prohibited
items.explanation: FMS LNAV operation: navigation shall not be predicated upon the UNS-1Esp during periods of dead reckoning (DR). Following DR, position should be verified by sighting ground reference points and/or by other navigation equipment such as NDB, VOR, DME or radar fix. The use of manually inserted runway coordinates is limited to VFR operations.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: FMS LNAV OPERATION (p.1-4)

items.question: If VNAV is to be used for an approach, when must en route VNAV be discontinued, and what is the primary altitude reference?
options: Within 5 nm of the FAF; the FMS computed altitude
At the FAF; the radar altimeter
Within 10 nm of the FAF; the pilot and copilot altimeters
Within 20 nm of the FAF; the GPS altitude
items.explanation: If VNAV is to be used for approach, use of en route VNAV must be discontinued within 10 nm of the FAF. When the approach mode is activated, as indicated by a green APP on the PFD, VNAV may be armed for the approach. Pilot and copilot altimeters are the primary altitude reference during all VNAV operations.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: FMS VNAV OPERATIONS (p.1-4)

items.question: An "INTEG" message appears on the PFD during an FMS approach. What does the RFM require?
options: Continue, since INTEG only means RAIM is recalculating
Discontinue navigation predicated on GPS
Switch the FMS to dead reckoning and continue to the MAP
Continue to the FAF, then decide whether RAIM is restored
items.explanation: If an "INTEG" message is displayed on the PFD during an approach, navigation predicated on GPS should be discontinued. RAIM must be available at the final approach fix to accomplish GPS based non-precision approaches; when RAIM is not available, INTEG is displayed on the PFD and "NO GPS RAIM @ FAF" or "NO GPS @ MAP" messages on the CDU.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: FMS APPROACHES (p.1-4)

items.question: Which approach operations with the FMS are not approved or not authorized?
options: GPS non-precision approaches and LNAV/VNAV approaches
RNAV approaches retrieved from the FMS database
GLS minimums and other WAAS operations, and ILS, LOC, LOC-BC, LDA, SDF and MLS approaches
GPS overlay VOR and NDB approaches
items.explanation: FMS approaches: operation in accordance with GLS approach minimums and other operations requiring WAAS are not approved. ILS, LOC, LOC-BC, LDA, SDF and MLS approaches are not authorized. The UNS-1Esp is approved for FMS VFR approaches as a VFR pilot aid only. Instrument approaches must be conducted in the approach mode prior to the FAF, as indicated by a green APP on the PFD.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: FMS APPROACHES (p.1-4)

items.question: Unless GPS approaches are approved for alternates by the operating rules, what must an alternate airport have?
options: At least two GPS approaches to different runways
A GPS approach with RAIM predicted at the ETA
An approach based on other than GPS, with the aircraft equipment and navaid operational
Nothing extra; any airport with a GPS approach may be an alternate
items.explanation: Unless GPS approaches are approved for alternate airports by applicable operating rules, airports selected as alternates must be served by an approach based on other than GPS navigation. The aircraft must have operational equipment capable of using that navigation aid, and the required navigation aid must be operational.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: FMS APPROACHES (p.1-4A)

items.question: Which of these is prohibited under the FLIGHT LIMITS?
options: 360° hovering turns in less than 6 seconds only
Hovering turns with more than 10 knots of wind
360° hovering turns in less than 12 seconds
Any hovering turn above 50 feet AGL
items.explanation: FLIGHT LIMITS: aerobatic maneuvers are prohibited; practice touchdown autorotations are prohibited; 360° hovering turns in less than 12 seconds are prohibited.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: FLIGHT LIMITS (p.1-5)

items.question: Which icing conditions are prohibited, and what is required for flight into approved icing conditions?
options: Only freezing rain is prohibited; RIPS is optional below 5,000 feet
Freezing drizzle, freezing rain and SLD are prohibited; RIPS must be on for icing conditions
All icing conditions are prohibited, with or without RIPS
SLD is approved with RIPS in OVRD; freezing rain is prohibited
items.explanation: Flight in freezing drizzle/freezing rain/supercooled large drops (SLD) is prohibited. For flight into icing conditions, the Rotor Ice Protection System (RIPS) must be turned on.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: FLIGHT LIMITS (p.1-5)

items.question: When may the OEI engine power ratings be used?
options: In an actual engine failure and in FADEC training mode
Only in the event of an actual engine failure
Whenever extra power is needed below 500 feet
For Category A takeoffs at maximum gross weight
items.explanation: Use of OEI engine power ratings except in the event of an actual engine failure is prohibited.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: FLIGHT LIMITS (p.1-5)

items.question: Which doors and windows may be open in flight?
options: Cockpit windows if latched fully open, and the upper cabin door and lower SAR door with equipment secured
The ramp and airstair door below 80 KIAS, with passengers seated
Cabin windows and cockpit windows, with loose equipment secured
None; all doors and windows must be closed in flight
items.explanation: Flight with the ramp, airstair door or cabin windows open is prohibited. The opening of cockpit windows in flight is authorized provided the window can be latched fully open and loose equipment is secured in the cockpit. Flight with the upper cabin sliding door and the lower (inward opening) SAR door open is authorized provided loose equipment is secured in the cabin and applicable airspeed limits are observed.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: FLIGHT LIMITS (p.1-5)

items.question: What limits apply to opening or closing the upper sliding door in flight?
options: 5° pitch up or down and 15° bank, with the cabin occupants standing clear
10° pitch up or down and 45° bank, with the ramp closed
No attitude limit, only an airspeed limit
10° pitch up or down and 30° bank, with all occupants seated and belted or harnessed
items.explanation: Maximum pitch attitude for opening or closing the upper sliding door is 10° nose up or down, and maximum bank angle is 30°. CAUTION: prior to inflight operations with a cabin door open, all cabin occupants must be seated with a seat belt fastened or restrained with an approved and properly adjusted harness.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: FLIGHT LIMITS (p.1-5)

items.question: When is carriage of passengers prohibited?
options: With the upper cabin sliding door open
With the lower search/rescue door installed
With the airstair door removed
With the rescue hoist installed
items.explanation: Carriage of passengers is prohibited with the installation of the lower search/rescue door.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: FLIGHT LIMITS (p.1-5)

items.question: What is the maximum demonstrated night Category A vertical Takeoff Decision Point (TDP)?
options: 200 feet
110 feet
50 feet
150 feet
items.explanation: Maximum demonstrated night Category A vertical Takeoff Decision Point (TDP) is 110 feet.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: FLIGHT LIMITS (p.1-5)

items.question: What is the minimum helipad size for Category A ground level helipad operations?
options: A 102 foot square
A 60 foot square
A 150 foot square
Twice the rotor diameter
items.explanation: Category A ground level helipad takeoffs and landings are flown in accordance with the Category A procedures in Section II and within the weight, altitude and temperature limits of Section IV. Minimum helipad size for Category A ground level helipad operations is a 102 foot square.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: FLIGHT LIMITS (p.1-5)

items.question: When is flight within the avoid area of the height-velocity diagram authorized?
options: During the Category A vertical ground level helipad takeoff and landing procedures, within their limits
During any Category B takeoff below 40 KIAS
Whenever the aircraft is below maximum takeoff weight
Never; the shaded area must always be avoided
items.explanation: Figure 1-1 (height-velocity diagram) NOTE: flight within the avoid area of the height-velocity diagram is authorized when conducting the Category A vertical ground level helipad takeoff and landing procedures described in Section II and when within the weight, altitude, temperature and wind limits for the applicable procedure.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: HEIGHT-VELOCITY DIAGRAM (p.1-6)

items.question: On helicopters with the flotation system, what does the RFM say about the life rafts and floats in flight?
options: Arming or deploying the life rafts and deploying the floats in flight are prohibited
Life rafts may be armed in flight, but floats must not be deployed
Floats may be deployed below 80 KIAS, but life rafts must not be armed
Both may be armed and deployed below 50 KIAS
items.explanation: FLIGHT LIMITS (FLOAT): arming or deploying the life rafts in flight is prohibited. Deploying the floats in flight is prohibited.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: FLIGHT LIMITS (p.1-7)

items.question: What are the maximum demonstrated IFR approach gradients?
options: 7.0° above 90 KIAS; 4.0° at or below 90 KIAS
3.0° above 90 KIAS; 6.0° at or below 90 KIAS
4.0° at all airspeeds
4.0° above 90 KIAS; 7.0° at or below 90 KIAS
items.explanation: The maximum demonstrated IFR approach gradient for airspeeds above 90 KIAS is 4.0°. The maximum demonstrated IFR approach gradient for airspeeds at or below 90 KIAS is 7.0°.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: FLIGHT LIMITS (p.1-7)

items.question: What is VNE power on, and what calculates the VNE shown on the PFD?
options: 150 KIAS; the FMS, from groundspeed and fuel weight
165 KIAS; the FADEC, from torque and Nr
180 KIAS; the air data computers, from outside air temperature only
165 KIAS; the air data computers, from temperature, pressure altitude and gross weight
items.explanation: VNE power on (maximum airspeed) is 165 KIAS. The air data computers automatically calculate VNE as a function of temperature, pressure altitude and gross weight for display on the airspeed indicator (PFD display mode).
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: AIRSPEED LIMITS (p.1-7)

items.question: What is the maximum airspeed with the landing gear down or in transit?
options: 120 KIAS
150 KIAS
90 KIAS
165 KIAS
items.explanation: Maximum airspeed with the landing gear down or in transit is 165 KIAS — the same as VNE power on. (The separate limit for activating the landing gear emergency blowdown is 90 KIAS.)
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: AIRSPEED LIMITS (p.1-7)

items.question: Which of these conditions does NOT limit the airspeed to 120 KIAS?
options: One or both SAS inoperative
Both autopilots inoperative
One primary flight control servo inoperative
Landing gear down or in transit
items.explanation: Maximum airspeed is 120 KIAS with one engine inoperative, one or both SAS inoperative, both APs inoperative, one primary flight control servo inoperative, the hydraulic boost inoperative, or any sliding door or window pinned open. With the landing gear down or in transit the maximum is 165 KIAS.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: AIRSPEED LIMITS (p.1-7)

items.question: What are the airspeed limits for flying with a sliding door or window pinned open, and for opening or closing it?
options: 80 KIAS pinned open; 120 KIAS to open or close
100 KIAS pinned open; 60 KIAS to open or close
120 KIAS for both
120 KIAS pinned open; 80 KIAS to open or close
items.explanation: Maximum airspeed with any sliding door or window pinned open is 120 KIAS. Maximum airspeed for opening or closing any sliding door or window is 80 KIAS. Both include the upper sliding SAR doors/windows, the inward opening lower door and the full length sliding door.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: AIRSPEED LIMITS (p.1-7)

items.question: What is the maximum airspeed with the floats armed?
options: 60 KIAS
90 KIAS
120 KIAS
80 KIAS
items.explanation: (FLOAT) Maximum airspeed with floats armed is 80 KIAS. After an inadvertent float deployment the limits are 50 KIAS in a climb, 55 KIAS in level flight and 60 KIAS in descent/autorotation.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: AIRSPEED LIMITS (p.1-7)

items.question: What is the maximum groundspeed for a normal landing or takeoff, and what follows a landing above it?
options: 50 knots; after landing faster, further flight and towing are prohibited, but taxiing is permitted
65 knots; after landing faster, taxiing and towing are prohibited
35 knots; after landing faster, an inspection is needed before taxiing
50 knots; after landing faster, one further flight to a maintenance base is permitted
items.explanation: Temporary Revision No. 3 (facing page 1-7) changes the limit to: maximum groundspeed for normal landing or takeoff is 50 knots (the basic page still shows 65 knots). NOTE: after landing in excess of 50 knots groundspeed, further flight and towing is prohibited. Taxi operations are permitted.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: AIRSPEED LIMITS (p.1-7 (Temporary Revision No. 3))

items.question: What is Vmini, the minimum airspeed for instrument flight?
options: 50 KIAS
35 KIAS
60 KIAS
70 KIAS
items.explanation: Vmini (minimum airspeed for instrument flight) is 50 KIAS.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: AIRSPEED LIMITS (p.1-7)

items.question: What are the maximum airspeeds for windshield wiper operation?
options: Standard wiper 40 knots; improved wiper 100 KIAS
Standard wiper 100 KIAS; improved wiper 165 KIAS
40 knots for both types
Standard wiper 80 KIAS; improved wiper 120 KIAS
items.explanation: Maximum airspeed for standard windshield wiper operations is 40 knots. Maximum airspeed for improved windshield wiper operations is 100 KIAS. The improved wiper arm has a stiffener inside the "U", visible from the cockpit.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: AIRSPEED LIMITS (p.1-8)

items.question: What are the limits for sideward flight or crosswind hover, and for rearward flight or tailwind hover?
options: 35 knots sideward; 20 knots rearward
20 knots sideward; 35 knots rearward
45 knots for both
35 knots for both
items.explanation: Maximum airspeed for sideward flight or crosswind hover is 35 knots. Maximum airspeed for rearward flight or tailwind hover is 35 knots.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: AIRSPEED LIMITS (p.1-8)

items.question: What is the maximum altitude for Category A ground level helipad operations?
options: 6,000 feet density altitude or 5,500 feet pressure altitude, whichever is higher
10,000 feet pressure altitude
5,500 feet density altitude or 6,000 feet pressure altitude, whichever is lower
15,000 feet density altitude
items.explanation: Maximum altitude for Category A ground level helipad operations is 5,500 feet density altitude or 6,000 feet pressure altitude, whichever is lower.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: ALTITUDE LIMITS (p.1-8)

items.question: What are the minimum altitudes for coupled operations?
options: 500 feet AGL above 120 KIAS; 200 feet AGL at or below 120 KIAS
200 feet AGL at all airspeeds
200 feet AGL above 120 KIAS; 50 feet AGL at or below 120 KIAS
100 feet AGL above 120 KIAS; 50 feet AGL at or below 120 KIAS
items.explanation: Minimum altitude for coupled operations with airspeed above 120 KIAS is 200 feet AGL. Minimum altitude for coupled operations with airspeed at or below 120 KIAS is 50 feet AGL.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: ALTITUDE LIMITS (p.1-8)

items.question: What applies to coupled flight at low height?
options: Below 200 feet AGL it must be in VMC; below 100 feet AGL it is prohibited
Below 200 feet AGL the pilot monitors the controls; below 100 feet AGL it must be in VMC
Below 100 feet AGL the pilot monitors the controls; below 50 feet AGL it must be in VMC
No additional requirements apply above 50 feet AGL
items.explanation: When coupled below 200 feet AGL, the pilot will monitor the flight controls and take action in the event of an excessive rate of descent. Coupled flight below 100 feet AGL will be in visual meteorological conditions.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: ALTITUDE LIMITS (p.1-8)

items.question: When is operation prohibited because of cold soaking, and how is airworthy status restored?
options: Engines shut down below -40°C for over 4 hours; warm at 0°C or above for 1 hour
Engines shut down below -25°C for over 1 hour; warm at 0°C or above for 8 hours, or use the pre-heat kit
Engines shut down below -17°C for over 1 hour; run the cold weather control exercise
Engines shut down below -25°C for over 8 hours; warm at 15°C or above for 2 hours
items.explanation: Operation is prohibited if the rotorcraft, with its engines shut down, is exposed to a ground ambient temperature below -25°C for a period longer than 1 hour. To restore airworthy status it should be warmed at or above 0°C (+32°F) for 8 hours, or the Cold Weather Pre-heat kit (P/N 92700-00110-011) must be used in accordance with the RFM Cold Weather Procedures.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: AMBIENT TEMPERATURE LIMITS (p.1-8)

items.question: Below what OAT should pitot heat and engine anti-ice be turned on?
options: Below 0°C
Below -5°C
Below 10°C
Below 5°C
items.explanation: Pitot heat and engine anti-ice should be turned on when OAT is less than 5°C.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: AMBIENT TEMPERATURE LIMITS (p.1-8)

items.question: What are the ECS limits for cockpit ventilation in flight?
options: MAX ACS only in flight above 30°C; recirculation on the ground only
Recirculation required in flight; MAX ACS at any time
Cockpit vent off whenever the air conditioning is on, in flight or on the ground
No MAX ACS or recirculation in flight (MAX ACS on the ground only); cockpit vent on if no heat or AC
items.explanation: To assure adequate fresh air ventilation to the cockpit when operating the air-conditioning system in flight, the cockpit temperature mode selection switch shall not be placed in the MAX ACS or recirculation position. The air-conditioning MAX ACS position is to be used on the ground only. If neither heat nor air-conditioning is used in flight, the cockpit vent must be on.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: ENVIRONMENTAL CONTROL SYSTEM LIMITS (p.1-8)

items.question: What is the minimum operating weight of the S-92?
items.explanation: Maximum takeoff and landing weight is 26,500 pounds (12,020 kg). Minimum operating weight is 16,200 pounds (7,348 kg). The helicopter is to be operated using the approved loading schedule (LOADING INFORMATION, RFM Part 2, Section II).
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: WEIGHT LIMITS (p.1-9)

items.question: On the Category A takeoff and landing gross weight charts, what is the minimum TDP speed with a crosswind component greater than 20 knots?
options: 30 KIAS
35 KIAS
60 KIAS
45 KIAS
items.explanation: Figure 1-2 (Cat 'A' Takeoff and Landing Gross Weight, all sheets) NOTE: with a crosswind component greater than 20 kts, the minimum TDP speed is 45 KIAS. The charts apply to 35 knots of crosswind component or less.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: CATEGORY 'A' OPERATIONS (p.1-10 to 1-12A (Figure 1-2))

items.question: The 30 minute dual engine rating (100% Q, 988°C TGT) applies to which flight condition?
options: Takeoff and climb only
Cruise above 100 KIAS only
Hovering flight only
Any flight condition, up to 30 minutes per flight
items.explanation: CT7-8A propulsion and drive system limits: 30 MIN rating, 30 minutes, 100% Q, 988°C TGT, 101.5% Ng. Note (2): the rating applies to hovering flight only.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: PROPULSION AND DRIVE SYSTEM LIMITS (p.1-18)

items.question: What are the single engine maximum continuous and 2 minute OEI torque and TGT limits?
options: Both 100% Q; TGT 935°C maximum continuous and 995°C for 2 minutes
120% and 141% Q; TGT 988°C and 1049°C
Both 120% Q; TGT 988°C maximum continuous and 1006°C for 2 minutes
Both 120% Q; TGT 1006°C maximum continuous and 1049°C for 2 minutes
items.explanation: Single engine limits: maximum continuous 120% Q, 988°C TGT, 102.4% Ng; OEI 2 minutes 120% Q, 1006°C TGT, 102.9% Ng; OEI 30 seconds 141% Q, 1049°C TGT, 103.7% Ng.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: PROPULSION AND DRIVE SYSTEM LIMITS (p.1-18)

items.question: What are the transient torque limits, dual engine and single engine?
options: Dual engine 110% for 12 seconds; single engine 141% for 30 seconds
Dual engine 116% for 12 seconds; single engine 150% for 10 seconds
Dual engine 120% for 5 seconds; single engine 156% for 10 seconds
Dual engine 120% for 10 seconds; single engine 156% for 5 seconds
items.explanation: Transient torque: dual engine 120% for 10 seconds; single engine 156% for 5 seconds. Note (3): these are associated with torque ramp up due to abnormal rotor droop at the FADEC controlled dual engine or OEI limit.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: PROPULSION AND DRIVE SYSTEM LIMITS (p.1-18)

items.question: What are the dual engine transient TGT limit and the maximum starting TGT?
options: 1049°C for 12 seconds; 935°C peak during start
1006°C for 10 seconds; 1049°C peak during start
1003°C for 12 seconds; 1000°C peak during start
995°C for 5 minutes; 1003°C peak during start
items.explanation: Dual engine TRANSIENT, 12 seconds: TGT 1003°C, Ng 103.7%, Np 116%. MAX. STARTING: peak TGT 1000°C.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: PROPULSION AND DRIVE SYSTEM LIMITS (p.1-18)

items.question: In the propulsion limits table, what do the shaded boxes mean, and what do the Q values represent?
options: Shaded boxes are pilot controlled limits; the Q values are engine limits
Shaded boxes are transient values; the Q values are power turbine limits
Shaded boxes are FADEC controlled limiter values; the Q values are gearbox limits
Shaded boxes are training mode values; the Q values are tail rotor limits
items.explanation: Table notes: a shaded box with a bold number denotes a FADEC controlled limiter value. Q (%) values are gearbox limits.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: PROPULSION AND DRIVE SYSTEM LIMITS (p.1-18)

items.question: Which component makes each of the Np/Nr avoid ranges critical?
options: 36 to 49%: engine power turbine. 56 to 67%: tail rotor drive shaft
36 to 49%: main rotor blades. 56 to 67%: main gearbox
Both ranges: the main rotor dampers
36 to 49%: tail rotor drive shaft. 56 to 67%: engine power turbine
items.explanation: Avoid prolonged operation in the following Np/Nr ranges: 36% to 49% (tail rotor drive shaft critical range) and 56% to 67% (engine power turbine critical range).
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: Np/Nr AVOID RANGES (p.1-18)

items.question: What are the engine oil pressure limits above idle?
options: Continuous 20 to 30 psi; maximum 100 psi for 15 minutes; fluctuation 10 psi maximum
Continuous 30 to 120 psi; maximum 150 psi for 5 minutes; no fluctuation limit
Continuous 30 to 100 psi; maximum 100 to 120 psi for 5 minutes; fluctuation 5 psi maximum
Continuous 45 to 100 psi; maximum 100 to 115 psi for 2 minutes; fluctuation 5 psi maximum
items.explanation: Engine oil pressure limits: min idle 20 to 30 psi; continuous 30 to 100 psi; maximum (5 min) 100 to 120 psi; max fluctuation 5 psi.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: ENGINE OIL PRESSURE LIMITS (p.1-19)

items.question: Before advancing the throttle to FLY, what must engine oil pressure be?
options: Above 30 psi
Below 120 psi
Below 100 psi
Between 20 and 30 psi
items.explanation: CAUTION: do not advance the throttle to FLY until oil pressure is below 100 psi. The pilot is permitted to make a slight throttle increase above IDLE to adjust Nr out of the lower avoid range.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: ENGINE OIL PRESSURE LIMITS (p.1-19)

items.question: What are the engine oil temperature limits?
options: 132°C continuous; 132 to 149°C for 15 minutes; 149°C maximum
130°C continuous; 130 to 140°C for 30 minutes; 140°C maximum
149°C continuous; 149 to 160°C for 5 minutes; 160°C maximum
120°C continuous; 120 to 132°C for 15 minutes; 132°C maximum
items.explanation: Engine oil temperature limits: max continuous 132°C; 15 minute 132° to 149°C; maximum allowable 149°C.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: ENGINE OIL TEMPERATURE LIMITS (p.1-19)

items.question: To what are fuel crossfeed operations limited in Category B?
options: Emergency operation only
Takeoff and landing only
Cruise flight only
No limit in Category B
items.explanation: Fuel crossfeed operations are limited to: Category A — emergency operation only; Category B — cruise flight only.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: FUEL CROSSFEED LIMITS (p.1-19)

items.question: What is required when changing from one approved fuel to another?
options: Draining the fuel system before the new fuel is added
No adjusting, draining or flushing of the fuel system
A FADEC fuel type adjustment by maintenance
Flushing the fuel system when changing between Jet A and JP-4
items.explanation: Approved fuels are Jet A, Jet A-1 and Jet B (ASTM D1655), No. 3 Jet Fuel (PRC GB6537), JP-5, JP-8 and JP-4. NOTE: no adjusting, draining, or flushing of the fuel system is required when changing from one fuel to another.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: APPROVED FUELS (p.1-19)

items.question: What are the fuel temperature limits for Jet B (JP-4)?
options: Maximum 57°C (135°F); minimum -40°C
Maximum 16°C (60°F); minimum -40°C
Maximum 16°C (60°F); minimum -20°C
Maximum 38°C (100°F); minimum -30°C
items.explanation: Fuel temperature limits: Jet A (JP-5, No. 3 Jet Fuel) and Jet A-1 (JP-8), maximum 57°C (135°F); Jet B (JP-4), maximum 16°C (60°F). Minimum for all three is -40°C (-40°F).
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: FUEL TEMPERATURE LIMITS (p.1-20)

items.question: What is the fuel quantity for a pressure refuel, and how much of the total is unusable?
options: 713 US gallons (2,700 L); 4.8 gallons (18 L) unusable
764 US gallons (2,890 L); 18 gallons (68 L) unusable
764 US gallons (2,890 L); 4.8 gallons (18 L) unusable
830 US gallons (3,140 L); 10 gallons (38 L) unusable
items.explanation: Fuel capacity: gravity refuel 713 US gallons (2,700 L); pressure refuel 764 US gallons (2,890 L). 4.8 gallons (18 liters) of total fuel quantity is unusable.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: FUEL CAPACITY (p.1-20)

items.question: Where in the flight envelope are engine starts in flight authorized?
options: Only below 150 KIAS, the same as the APU
Only below 10,000 feet pressure altitude
Throughout the complete aircraft operating envelope
Only between 80 and 120 KIAS
items.explanation: Engine starts in flight are authorized throughout the complete aircraft operating envelope. APU starts and continuous operation are restricted to airspeeds less than 150 KIAS.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: ENGINE AND APU INFLIGHT STARTING (p.1-22)

items.question: Dual engine torque reaches 115% for 15 seconds. What does the drive system limits table require?
options: No inspection
Removal and replacement of the MGB
A serviceability check
A serviceability check only if it lasted more than 30 seconds
items.explanation: Drive system limits, dual engine: 0 to 100% continuous; 101 to 120% — no inspection required under 10 seconds, serviceability check above 10 seconds; 121 to 140% — serviceability check under 10 seconds, remove/replace MGB above 10 seconds; above 140% — remove/replace MGB on any occurrence.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: DRIVE SYSTEM LIMITS (p.1-23)

items.question: Dual engine torque exceeds 140%, however briefly. What does the drive system limits table require?
options: A serviceability check
Removal and replacement of the MGB
No inspection if it lasted less than 10 seconds
A serviceability check if it lasted more than 5 seconds
items.explanation: Drive system limits, dual engine: above 140% torque requires removal/replacement of the MGB on any occurrence. (Single engine, the same applies above 156%.)
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: DRIVE SYSTEM LIMITS (p.1-23)

items.question: Single engine torque reaches 135%. For how long may it last with no inspection required?
options: Less than 30 seconds
Less than 10 seconds
Less than 5 seconds
Less than 2 minutes
items.explanation: Drive system limits, single engine: 0 to 120% continuous; 121 to 141% — no inspection under 30 seconds, serviceability check above 30 seconds; 142 to 156% — serviceability check under 5 seconds, remove/replace MGB above 5 seconds; above 156% — remove/replace MGB on any occurrence.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: DRIVE SYSTEM LIMITS (p.1-23)

items.question: What are the continuous and precautionary MGB oil temperature ranges?
options: Continuous 0 to 120°C; precautionary 120 to 130°C
Continuous 0 to 130°C; precautionary 130 to 149°C
Continuous 20 to 110°C; precautionary 110 to 120°C
Continuous 0 to 132°C; precautionary 132 to 149°C
items.explanation: MGB oil temperature limits: continuous 0° to 120°C; precautionary 120° to 130°C; maximum 130°C.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: MGB OIL TEMPERATURE LIMITS (p.1-23)

items.question: With Nr at or above 80% or the aircraft airborne, what is the continuous MGB oil pressure range, and what is the maximum?
options: Continuous 30 to 70 psi; maximum 100 psi
Continuous 35 to 45 psi; maximum 70 psi
Continuous 45 to 70 psi; maximum 130 psi
Continuous 45 to 100 psi; maximum 130 psi
items.explanation: MGB oil pressure, Nr at or above 80% or aircraft in the air: minimum 35 psi; precautionary 35 to 45 psi; continuous 45 to 70 psi; precautionary 70 to 130 psi; maximum 130 psi.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: MGB OIL PRESSURE LIMITS (p.1-23)

items.question: What are the power on maximum rotor speed and its precautionary range?
options: 106% maximum; 104 to 106% precautionary
110% maximum; 106 to 110% precautionary
115% maximum; 110 to 115% precautionary
110% maximum; 105 to 110% precautionary
items.explanation: Rotor speed limits, power on: maximum 110%; precautionary range 106% to 110%; normal operating rotor speed dual engine 104% to 106%, OEI 100% to 106%.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: ROTOR SPEED LIMITS (p.1-24)

items.question: What are the power on low rotor speed ranges, dual engine and OEI?
options: Normal OEI 100 to 106%; precautionary 95 to 104% dual and 95 to 100% OEI; minimum 95%
Normal OEI 104 to 106%; precautionary 90 to 104% dual and 90 to 100% OEI; minimum 90%
Normal OEI 100 to 106%; precautionary 96 to 104% for both; minimum 96%
Normal OEI 95 to 106%; no precautionary range; minimum 80%
items.explanation: Rotor speed limits, power on: normal operating rotor speed OEI 100% to 106% (dual engine 104% to 106%); precautionary range dual engine 95% to 104%, OEI 95% to 100%; minimum 95%; transient minimum OEI 90%; transient at touchdown during OEI landing 80%.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: ROTOR SPEED LIMITS (p.1-24)

items.question: What are the power off (autorotation) maximum and transient minimum rotor speeds?
options: Maximum 106%; transient minimum 90%
Maximum 110%; transient minimum 80%
Maximum 115%; transient minimum 85%
Maximum 110%; transient minimum 95%
items.explanation: Rotor speed limits, power off: maximum 110%; minimum ("LOW ROTOR" aural alert) 95%; transient minimum 80%.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: ROTOR SPEED LIMITS (p.1-24)

items.question: With the rotor brake on and the rotor stopped, what engine operation is allowed?
options: One engine only, up to FLY
One or both engines at idle only
No engine operation at all
Both engines up to 50% Nr equivalent power
items.explanation: ROTOR BRAKE LIMITS, ROTOR STOPPED: engine operation is limited to one or both engines at idle.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: ROTOR BRAKE LIMITS (p.1-25)

items.question: What is the recommended rotor speed for a normal rotor brake application?
options: 50% Nr or below
25% Nr or below
Up to 105% Nr
40% Nr or below
items.explanation: Recommended rotor speed for normal rotor brake application is 40% Nr or below. Maximum rotor speed for an emergency rotor brake application with both engines shut down is 105% Nr. Both engines must be shut down before applying the rotor brake.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: ROTOR BRAKE LIMITS (p.1-25)

items.question: What is the depress mode pressure of the #3 hydraulic system?
options: 4200 psi
items.explanation: Hydraulic system limits: depress (system 3 only) 2000 ± 1000 psi; minimum 3500 psi; normal 3500 to 4200 psi; maximum 4200 psi.
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: HYDRAULIC SYSTEM LIMITS (p.1-25)

items.question: What are the dual engine Ng limits?
options: 100% continuous; 102.4% for 30 minutes; 103.7% for 5 minutes takeoff; 108.5% for 12 seconds
99.9% continuous; 101.5% for 30 minutes; 102.9% for 5 minutes takeoff; 103.7% for 12 seconds
99.9% continuous; 102.9% for 30 minutes; 103.7% for 5 minutes takeoff; 105% for 12 seconds
102.4% continuous; 102.9% for 30 minutes; 103.7% for 5 minutes takeoff; 108.5% for 12 seconds
items.explanation: Ng limits, dual engine (Figure 1-6 and the propulsion limits table): 99.9% maximum continuous (green); 101.5% for 30 minutes and 102.9% for 5 minutes takeoff (yellow); 103.7% 12 second transient (red).
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: INSTRUMENT MARKINGS (p.1-28 (Figure 1-6 Sheet 3))

items.question: What are the single engine Ng limits?
options: 99.9% continuous; 101.5% for 2 minutes; 102.9% for 30 seconds
102.9% continuous; 103.7% for 2 minutes; 108.5% for 30 seconds
102.4% continuous; 103.7% for 2 minutes; 105.0% for 30 seconds
102.4% continuous; 102.9% for 2 minutes; 103.7% for 30 seconds
items.explanation: Ng limits, single engine: 102.4% maximum continuous (green); 102.9% for 2 minutes and 103.7% for 30 seconds (yellow).
references: S-92 RFM Part 1 Sec I: INSTRUMENT MARKINGS (p.1-28 (Figure 1-6 Sheet 3))
